loading="lazy"></picture><figcaption><!--[--><!--[--><p><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><b>Conceptual model of biological and ecosystem properties governing microbial community resistance to and resilience after disturbance</b><!--]-->. Stability of microbial communities in the face of disturbances is influenced by individual-, population-, and community-level biological attributes that contribute to community resistance (left, green background) and/or resilience (right, blue background), or both (center). Individuals withstand or survive disturbances and promote persistence of populations, which in turn promote overall community stability (orange arrows). Ecosystem drivers (leftmost blue boxes), such as trophic structure and disturbance regime, shape biological attributes, and also contribute to resistance and resilience. Finally, we hypothesize that biological attributes will be differently advantageous given a pulse (orange or purple) or press (purple) disturbance.</p><!--]--><!--]--></figcaption></figure></button></div><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h3>Individual properties: Plasticity, stress tolerance, and dormancy</h3><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h4>Plasticity and stress response</h4><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Resistance to compositional change in the face of disturbances is enhanced if a microbial community contains many individuals that have versatile physiologies, or physiological plasticity (Evans and Hofmann, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B40-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B40a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></span>). Bacteria often navigate environmental change by expressing a range of metabolic capabilities (e.g., Meyer et al., <a href="#B103" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2004<!--]--></a>; Swingley et al., <a href="#B145" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2007<!--]--></a>), and therefore the existing community can confront new conditions through gene expression by individual cells. From an evolutionary standpoint, adaptive gene expression refers to natural selection acting on gene expression (Whitehead and Crawford, <a href="#B162" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>), and this phenomenon has been observed, for example, in a yeast model of experimental evolution (Ferea et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B43-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B43a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->1999<!--]--></span>). Furthermore, mixotrophy, or the ability to use many different carbon and energy sources, may be a common phenomenon in natural microbial communities (Eiler, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B35-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B35a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></span>), and provides further support for the notion of individual flexibility in fluctuating environments. Cellular stress responses also provide protection for individual cells from damaging physical factors such as reactive oxygen species, temperature, and ultraviolet light (e.g., Craig, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B26-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B26a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->1985<!--]--></span>; Ziegelhoffer and Donohue, <a href="#B172" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>; Kolowrat et al., <a href="#B78" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>). Stress protection in <!--[--><i>E. coli</i><!--]--> is associated with a progressive decrease in nutritional competence, or the breadth and range of carbon and nutrient resources that a cell can use (Ferenci, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B44-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B44a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2005<!--]--></span>; Ferenci and Spira, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B45-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B45a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2007<!--]--></span>), which ultimately may reduce the population’s ability to confront other environmental changes. Therefore, there may be fitness costs to microbial stress responses that are manifested in seemingly unrelated metabolic pathways, or costs of maximizing protection against one stress over another. Stress tolerance can contribute to microbial community resistance to pulse or press disturbances, but will depend on the intensity and duration of the disturbance relative to an individual’s levels of stress tolerance (Figure <a href="#F4" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->4<!--]--></a>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Compositional stability is mediated, in part, by the ability of individual microorganisms to respond to, accommodate, and exploit environmental change. This highlights a difference between microbial communities and communities of larger organisms: prokaryotes have a degree of physiological plasticity that is unparalleled in the eukaryotic world. The unique ability to shift to an entirely different lifestyle within a short time (as in the classic example of <!--[--><i>Rhodobacter sphaeroides</i><!--]-->, which can grow anaerobically as a phototroph but also grow aerobically as a chemoheterotroph) is likely to increase the compositional stability while simultaneously reducing the functional stability. Current ecological theory based on plants and animals may not accommodate the enormous physiological plasticity of prokaryotes, which may necessitate development of new principles applicable to microbial communities. We hypothesize that physiological plasticity can contribute to a microbial community’s resistance and resilience to either pulse or press disturbances. But, similar to stress tolerance, the contribution of plasticity to community stability will depend on the intensity and duration of the disturbance relative to an individual’s physiological response.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h4>Dormancy</h4><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Dormancy is a bet-hedging strategy that allows organisms to enter a reduced state of metabolic activity (Jones and Lennon, <a href="#B74" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>); see Lennon and Jones, <a href="#B88" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></a> for a recent review). A substantial fraction of community members may be dormant or inactive at any given moment (e.g., Pedrós-Alío, <a href="#B111" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>; Jones and Lennon, <a href="#B74" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>). Dormancy strategies may be common among communities living in temporally dynamic environments, promoting overall compositional stability in fluctuating conditions. Furthermore, the proportion of inactive taxa (and, inactive individuals within a taxon) may signify important environmental differences among communities from similar habitats, as shown, for example, in gut microbial communities from humans with and without irritable bowel syndrome (Rehman et al., <a href="#B119" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Dormancy has most likely evolved across the tree of life as a means for contending with temporarily variable environments. It is an advantageous strategy under unpredictable conditions because it allows individuals to maximize their long-term, geometric fitness (de Jong et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B28-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B28a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></span>). Recent studies suggest that, in a wide range of ecosystems, a substantial fraction of microbial communities may be metabolically inactive (Lennon and Jones, <a href="#B88" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></a>). This observation has important implications for the resistance and resilience of microbial communities. First, on a population-level, dormancy may prevent the extinction of certain taxa from a system. For example, active individuals of <!--[--><i>E. coli</i><!--]--> succumb when exposed to certain antibiotics. However, the population can ultimately be rescued, not necessarily by the survival of mutants, but rather by subpopulations of dormant persister cells that become reactivated when antibiotic effects are attenuated (Lewis, <a href="#B91" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>). Evidence suggests that microorganisms may use dormancy in a variety of other situations as well, for example when challenged by unfavorable temperatures (Whitesides and Oliver, <a href="#B163" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1997<!--]--></a>), starvation (del Giorgio and Gasol, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B31-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B31a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></span>), or predator-induced mortality (Pearl et al., <a href="#B110" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>). Second, dormancy has the potential to affect the stability of communities and ecosystem processes. Dormant individuals can be long-lived and contribute to seed banks. It is well documented that seed banks can maintain species diversity (Chesson, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B21-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2000<!--]--></span>), and this diversity may directly contribute to stability of microbial communities via niche complementation and/or functional redundancy (Loreau and Hector, <a href="#B97" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2001<!--]--></a>; Petchey and Gaston, <a href="#B112" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2002<!--]--></a>). Seed banks may also aid in the recovery of microbial communities from severe disturbance events. For example, dormant seeds often contribute to the reestablishment of plant communities following fire, flooding, or wind storms (Bond and Midgley, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B13-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B13a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2001<!--]--></span>). In many cases, microbial communities show similar signs of rapid recovery following catastrophic disturbances (Jones et al., <a href="#B73" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>; Shade et al., <a href="#B135" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>). Although dormancy may contribute to the stability of these communities, this remains to be tested.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>We propose that dormancy is more important for maintaining community stability under pulse disturbance scenarios (Figure <a href="#F4" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->4<!--]--></a>), as dormancy would be advantageous in a temporarily disturbed ecosystem, but likely less so in a continuously disturbed ecosystem. The exception to this would be a long-lived seed bank of dormant cells that is sustained beyond the effects of a press disturbance. Also, depending on the specific ecosystem changes caused by a press disturbance, environmental cues for “waking” from dormancy (Epstein, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B39-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B39a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></span>) may be altered or absent if a disturbance is continuous.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h3>Population properties: Adaptation, growth rate, stochastic expression, and dispersal</h3><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h4>Evolutionary adaptation</h4><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Microorganisms generally feature rapid growth, high population densities, and high mutation rates and are capable of recombination via lateral gene transfer, which facilitates response to disturbance events (e.g., Lenski and Bennett, <a href="#B90" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1993<!--]--></a>). As such, disturbance often can provide selection pressure that drives diversification (Travisano and Rainey, <a href="#B150" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1998<!--]--></a>; Cohan, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B23-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B23a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2002<!--]--></span>). A number of studies have shown that rapid evolution of population traits can influence the temporal dynamics of microbial communities. For example, microbial predator-prey dynamics are strongly affected by selection (Yoshida et al., <a href="#B170" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></a>), especially for traits that provide defense against predators (Little and Currie, <a href="#B94" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>). Also, rapid evolution can counterbalance the top-down effects of a novel predator on nutrient cycling. For example, viruses introduced into continuous cultures of the picocyanobacterium <!--[--><i>Synechococcus</i><!--]--> dramatically reduced population densities, thereby increasing availability of the growth-limiting resource, phosphorus. However, <!--[--><i>Synechococcus</i><!--]--> population densities rebounded with the growth of a virus-resistant <!--[--><i>Synechococcus</i><!--]--> mutant. Host resistance coincided with reduced nutrient availability (Lennon and Martiny, <a href="#B89" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>). Together these studies suggest that rapid evolution is an important mechanism of compositional and functional resistance and resilience to certain disturbances, and is particularly important for response to press disturbances (Cohan, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B23-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B23a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2002<!--]--></span>). By contrast, there may be advantages of bet-hedging strategies, such as phenotypic plasticity or dormancy, to contend with disturbance in systems that experience transient pulse disturbances. Adaptability is likely important for microbial community resistance and resilience given repeated pulse disturbances (such as in a disturbance regime, e.g., fire or flooding), as well as press disturbances (Figure <a href="#F4" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->4<!--]--></a>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h4>Growth rate</h4><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>A tradeoff between growth rate and resource use efficiency (and hence competitive ability) may underlie the capacity of microbial populations to respond to disturbance (Stevenson and Schmidt, <a href="#B141" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2004<!--]--></a>). Enhanced growth rate is accompanied by a higher rate of synthesis of ribosomal components and is faster in microorganisms with more copies of rRNA-encoding genes, reducing the response time to favorable growth conditions for such organisms. When pulse disturbances are followed by favorable growth conditions, the fastest responders will multiply and alter community composition (Klappenbach et al., <a href="#B75" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2000<!--]--></a>), resulting in low resistance. By contrast, microorganisms with fewer copies of rRNA-encoding genes maximize efficiency of resource use (progeny per mole substrate; Lee et al., <a href="#B85" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>), and may increase community resistance to press disturbances that result in long-term resource limitation. Genes other than rRNA genes distinguish bacteria optimized to grow at high nutrient (copiotrophic) and low nutrient (oligotrophic) conditions (Lauro et al., <a href="#B83" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>). While the identity of rapid responders may be idiosyncratic across environments, quantifying the capacity of a microbial community for rapid growth or efficient resource utilization could inform hypotheses regarding each community’s compositional responses to pulse and press disturbances. Growth rate likely is important for microbial community resilience from pulse disturbances, as a few surviving individuals could grow quickly to recover to pre-disturbance population sizes after a sudden pulse, mortality-inducing disturbance, especially if the disturbance makes new resources available.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>The relative growth rates of interacting microbial communities also can have implications for microbial resilience and resistance to press disturbances. A recent study compared the drought responses of a fungal-based food web in grassland soil with that of a bacterial-based food web in agricultural soil (de Vries et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B29-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B29a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></span>). The results of this study suggested that relatively slower-growing fungi were more resistant to drought, but less resilient, while relatively faster-growing bacteria were less resistant but more resilient. The authors built structural models to assess the impact of fungal and bacterial drought responses on microarthropod (grazers of bacteria and fungi) richness, soil respiration, nitrogen dioxide production, and nitrogen leaching. This study demonstrated that press disturbances that alter microbial food webs may also influence soil resource availability. It also showed that the stability of microbial food webs was contingent, at least in part, on the ratio of slower-growing fungi to faster-growing bacteria.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h4>Stochastic gene expression</h4><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Another means by which a microbial population can respond quickly to environmental change is through stochastic gene expression (Avery, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B6-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B6a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></span>; Raj and van Oudenaarden, <a href="#B116" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>), a process that samples multiple phenotypes and hence, like dormancy, is also considered a bet-hedging strategy. The presence of persister cells – dormant variants within a bacterial population that are tolerant to antibiotics (e.g., Lewis, <a href="#B92" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>) – is one example of an alternative phenotype that increases fitness in an environment experiencing a transient selective pressure. Stochastic gene expression is among the multiple pathways that can lead to the formation of persisters (Lewis, <a href="#B92" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>), a phenomenon that may have many parallels in non-pathogenic microorganisms. Stochastic gene expression may be key for microbial community resistance to pulse disturbances, as it offers a short-term strategy for survival of individuals that can re-populate a community after disturbance.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h4>Dispersal and immigration</h4><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>The large population sizes and rapid dispersal abilities (e.g., Finlay, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B46-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B46a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2002<!--]--></span>) of microorganisms can play an important role in community recovery after disturbance. Dispersal is a key feature of metacommunity theory, which recognizes communities as collections of interacting local communities linked by the movement of individuals in heterogeneous landscapes (e.g., Leibold et al., <a href="#B86" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2004<!--]--></a>; Logue et al., <a href="#B96" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></a>). Disturbances initiate iterations of community re-assembly by killing or inactivating local resident taxa, releasing resources, and creating empty niches. These empty niches can be filled by local taxa (resistant taxa or taxa retrieved from seed banks) or by immigrants that arrive from other localities within a metacommunity.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Colonists dispersed from nearby localities (patches) can “re-seed” microbial populations that have become locally extinct after disturbance, thereby facilitating community resilience (Figure <a href="#F4" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->4<!--]--></a>). For example, freshwater bacterial communities disturbed by a pulse salinity increase were both compositionally and functionally resilient because of continuous dispersal of microorganisms from an undisturbed source community (Baho et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B7-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B7a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></span>). As another example, protozoan and rotifer population densities were more resilient after a recurring pulse disturbance (replacing 99% of a mesocosm’s contents with sterile media) when the disturbed mesocosm was connected to an undisturbed one (Altermatt et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B3-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011a<!--]--></span>) than when the disturbed mesocosm had no refuge.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>On the other hand, if disturbances are wide-spread such that they affect entire regions (e.g., climate effects, such as heat waves), dispersal could promote the dissemination of disturbance-tolerant taxa among localities (Eggers et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B34-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B34a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></span>), thereby changing the dominant membership of a community and decreasing overall community resilience at both local and regional scales. For example, marine microalgae communities disturbed by a simulated heat wave were sensitive but not resilient because of a shift in community dominance toward a temperature-tolerant species. This species also became prevalent in other patches connected by dispersal, even though the conditions there were less suitable for it (Eggers et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B34-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B34a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></span>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Furthermore, niches opened by disturbance events are subject to stochastic colonization events by dispersed microorganisms. “<!--[--><i>Priority effects</i><!--]-->” refers to the impact that successful early colonizers may have on community re-assembly after disturbance, which can affect the likelihood of colonization by subsequently dispersed microorganisms (e.g., Shulman et al., <a href="#B137" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1983<!--]--></a>). Early post-disturbance colonizers that adapt rapidly to local conditions may persist long-term, out-competing native community members and impeding community resilience (Urban and De Meester, <a href="#B152" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Together these studies and others demonstrate that microbial dispersal, in interaction with biological attributes of local resident populations (plasticity, dormancy, or evolution) and disturbance characteristics, can have important implications for the resilience of microbial communities.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h3>Community properties: Diversity, turnover, and emergent properties</h3><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h4>Diversity in all of its forms</h4><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>In general, diversity is thought to influence how communities respond to disturbance. Aspects of alpha diversity, such as species richness and evenness, have been shown to enhance the functional resilience of communities of larger organisms (Allison, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B1-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B1a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2004<!--]--></span>; Downing and Leibold, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B33-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></span>; Van Ruijven and Berendse, <a href="#B155" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>), whereas evidence about the impact of richness and evenness on microbial community resilience is mixed (e.g., Griffiths et al., <a href="#B60" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2000a<!--]--></a>; Wertz et al., <a href="#B159" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2007<!--]--></a>; Wittebolle et al., <a href="#B166" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>; van Elsas et al., <a href="#B154" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>One challenge lies in clarifying the functional and compositional responses to disturbances of diverse communities. The underlying mechanisms behind a positive relationship between taxon diversity and resilience may be related to a buffering effect, called the <!--[--><i>Insurance Hypothesis</i><!--]--> (Yachi and Loreau, <a href="#B169" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1999<!--]--></a>). More genetically diverse communities are more likely to contain taxa with complementary response traits (e.g., Tilman et al., <a href="#B148" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1997<!--]--></a>, <a href="#B149" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>; Lavorel and Garnier, <a href="#B84" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2002<!--]--></a>; Elmqvist et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B38-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B38a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2003<!--]--></span>) and the ability for rapid compensatory growth after a disturbance (e.g., Flöder et al., <a href="#B47" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>), which may promote resilience. Also, rare microbial taxa (potentially below the limit of detection, and therefore not counted in estimates of community diversity) may quickly respond to altered environmental conditions and become abundant. This is exemplified by the case of a rare <!--[--><i>Vibrio</i><!--]--> species that was below detection in the majority of the time points over a 6-year study in the Western English Channel, but then bloomed to become a prevalent member of the community at one time point (Caporaso et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B17-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B17a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></span>). Co-occurrence networks were used to find that the <!--[--><i>Vibrio</i><!--]--> bloom was correlated to a bloom of a diatom species (Gilbert et al., <a href="#B55" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>). Though models are constantly improved for predicting conditions for microbial blooms (Larsen et al., <a href="#B82" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>), niche spaces for many environmental microorganisms remain uncharacterized, which further veils the relationship between compositional and functional diversity and microbial community stability.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Here we discuss a few examples (of many in the literature) of the impact of diversity on microbial community stability. In an early experiment to tease apart the relations between diversity and community functions, Griffiths et al. (<a href="#B61" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2000b<!--]--></a>) examined the impact of soil microbial diversity on functional stability using a range of intensities of soil fumigation followed by a disturbance, either a heat shock (pulse disturbance) or the addition of the heavy metal copper (II) sulfate (press disturbance). The results indicated that microbial production (rate of generation of biomass, here measured as thymidine incorporation) was not affected, but specific functions, such as nitrification, decreased when diversity was lower. The lower-diversity communities were less functionally resistant (measured as grass residue decomposition rate) to the press disturbance and unable to recover, but were sometimes more resistant to the pulse disturbance than the higher-diversity communities. The control community, which was not fumigated and had the highest diversity, was often the most resilient to both pulse and press disturbances.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Building on the Griffiths et al. (<a href="#B61" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2000b<!--]--></a>) results, the relationship between species richness and stability was investigated for denitrifiers and nitrite oxidizers (Wertz et al., <a href="#B159" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2007<!--]--></a>), two specialized functional groups of soil microorganisms important for nitrogen cycling. In this work, microbial abundance (and, as an extension, richness) was altered by inoculating soil microcosms with different dilutions of microbial cells from non-sterile soil. After a period of incubation, the microcosms were subjected to a pulse heating disturbance. Denaturing gel gradient electrophoresis fingerprints of the denitrifiers and the nitrite oxidizers were coupled with measurements of the two processes, and each responded differently to heating. Though both processes were sensitive, denitrification was resilient after 3 months, while nitrite oxidation did not completely recover. The response of richness to heating was variable across dilutions, and richness did not recover to pre-disturbance levels after 3 months. These results suggest that a community may recover in function even if diversity remains altered after disturbance, and that the initial richness may not necessarily impact functional recovery.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>A microcosm experiment was performed to specifically examine the role of initial community evenness (equitability of taxa abundances) on functional stability of denitrifiers subjected to a press increase in salinity and temperature (Wittebolle et al., <a href="#B166" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>). The authors found that high initial evenness was important for functional stability of microbial communities. However, the communities were not observed after the disturbance ceased to assess resilience of function or evenness. This work demonstrated that aspects of diversity other than species richness can play a role for community functional stability. Given that many environmental microbial communities are characteristically uneven because they contain a large number of rare taxa (sometimes referred to as the “rare biosphere,” e.g., Casamayor et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B20-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B20a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2001<!--]--></span>; Sogin et al., <a href="#B139" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>), the implications of small differences in evenness among generally uneven communities may be of interest for further investigation.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>A very recent experiment demonstrated the impact of diversity on stability by creating synthetic combinations of soil isolates, rather than confronting the complexity and unknown organisms of the natural soil (van Elsas et al., <a href="#B154" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>). With constructed mixtures containing various numbers of random representatives of a collection of cultured isolates, the authors demonstrated a highly significant correlation between species richness of the community and its resistance to invasion by an <!--[--><i>E. coli</i><!--]--> strain (van Elsas et al., <a href="#B154" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>).</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Together, these studies and others reveal the complex relationships between microbial community diversity, function, and stability. Multiple aspects of diversity (richness, evenness) can affect microbial functional resistance and resilience, and general and specific community functions may have different overall responses to pulse disturbance. Importantly, these studies suggest that there may not be a “one-size-fits-all” response of microbial diversity and function to disturbance. For diversity-stability relations, more work must be done to understand system-specific trends before it will be possible to determine which patterns, if any, are general across microbial systems.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h4>Compositional turnover</h4><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Community turnover is the replacement and substitution of community members along an environmental gradient or with time (Wilson and Shmida, <a href="#B165" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1984<!--]--></a>). Turnover is directed by the growth of populations, and partially determines how quickly a community recovers from a pulse disturbance (Figure <a href="#F4" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->4<!--]--></a>). High-throughput fingerprinting and sequencing tools that enable experiments involving longer time series demonstrate that many microbial communities have clear trajectories. For example, successional patterns have been observed in tree leaf bacterial communities over the growing season (Redford and Fierer, <a href="#B118" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>; Redford et al., <a href="#B117" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>), in the human gut after antibiotic treatment (Antonopoulos et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B5-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B5a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></span>; Dethlefsen and Relman, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B32-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B32a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></span>), and in the infant gut during the first two and a half years of development (Koenig et al., <a href="#B77" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></a>). Also, seasonal trajectories are common in freshwater, marine, and sediment systems (Fuhrman et al., <a href="#B51" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>; Christian and Lind, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B22-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B22a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2007<!--]--></span>; Shade et al., <a href="#B133" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2007<!--]--></a>; Nelson, <a href="#B106" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>; Andersson et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B4-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></span>; Crump et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B27-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B27a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></span>; Gilbert et al., <a href="#B53" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>, <a href="#B54" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>). Together these studies provide insight into the temporal scale on which community turnover and disturbance responses may be anticipated in similar systems, but turnover is unknown for many other habitats. Further investigation is needed to describe, quantify, and compare turnover within and across habitats.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Species-time relationships, which quantify the accumulation of new species in a community with time, provide a method to calculate community turnover (White et al., <a href="#B161" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>). There is preliminary evidence that species-time relationships of community turnover may be common among microbial communities from very different environments. For example, microbial communities in streams (Portillo et al., <a href="#B115" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>), on leaf surfaces (Redford et al., <a href="#B117" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>), across a set of newly deglaciated soils (Nemergut et al., <a href="#B107" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2007<!--]--></a>), and in bioreactors (Van Der Gast et al., <a href="#B153" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>), have exhibited species-time relationships with turnover rates comparable to those of larger organisms. If most microbial communities display a characteristic turnover rate, as observed for communities of larger organisms (White et al., <a href="#B161" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>), variation around the expected range of community turnover rates may be a reasonable starting point for comparing microbial community responses to disturbance.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Similarity-decay (Nekola and White, <a href="#B105" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1999<!--]--></a>) is a common method for understanding changes in microbial community structure over space (e.g., Horner-Devine et al., <a href="#B66" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2004<!--]--></a>; Jones et al., <a href="#B72" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>), but has also been applied over time in communities of larger organisms (Korhonen et al., <a href="#B80" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>). For temporal similarity-decay, all pairs of community resemblance (<!--[--><i>a.k.a</i><!--]-->. similarity or distance) are regressed against time (or space) between community observations. The slope of this regression is analogous to a turnover rate, but has additional utility from species-time relationships because the resemblance metric can be chosen to include properties of community composition (e.g., Sørensen), structure (e.g., Bray–Curtis), and phylogenetic representation (e.g., UniFrac distance, based on the underlying calculation of phylogenetic diversity, Faith, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B41-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B41a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->1992<!--]--></span>). Similarity-decay has been applied to understand temporal dynamics of microbial communities (e.g., Wittebolle et al., <a href="#B167" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>; Bürgmann et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B16-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B16a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></span>). As one example, similarity-decay was used to compare resilience of lake microbial communities across treatments in an experiment designed to separate the environmental drivers of oxygen and nutrients from the physical process of water column mixing, an important seasonal disturbance to temperate lake bacterial communities (Shade et al., <a href="#B134" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></a>). In this study, similarity-decay relationships were used in part to quantify the relative robustness of the communities to these environmental disturbances, such that the hypolimnion community was found to be the most sensitive to oxygen addition, but also the most resilient. Though similarity-decay clearly is useful as a baseline descriptor of temporal community turnover, this study demonstrated the additional utility of similarity-decay for comparing microbial community resilience when challenged with different disturbances.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><!--[--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><h4>Emergent properties: microbial communities as networks</h4><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Interactions between community members, including competition and mutualism (Little et al., <a href="#B95" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2008<!--]--></a>), are also important in determining community response to disturbances. For example, a mesocosm experiment with protist communities demonstrated that competitive interactions and disturbance characteristics together determined the community disturbance response, where competition between species became increasingly important in driving extinction as the intensity of disturbance was amplified (Violle et al., <a href="#B158" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>). This trend was observed despite the fact that the species were chosen for the experiment because they collectively represented a wide range of competitive ability and disturbance tolerance. Thus, the community response was more complex than the sum of the individual species’ traits, and instead hinged on interspecific interactions.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>As time series analyses of microbial communities become increasingly available, we will be better able to quantify complex interactions among community members. For instance, recently developed statistical tools enable investigation of microbial interactions by studying co-occurrences of microbial taxa through time. Networks can be built from co-occurrences, with nodes representing taxa or operational taxonomic units (OTUs) and connecting edges representing correlation over time (e.g., Ruan et al., <a href="#B124" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>). These networks assess effects of disturbance on community dynamics (Montoya et al., <a href="#B104" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>). Positive co-occurrence may indicate common preferred environmental conditions or cooperative activities (facilitation and/or syntrophy). Similarly, negative correlations may represent the outcome of competition (i.e., displacement) or negative interactions, such as allelopathy or predation (Fuhrman, <a href="#B50" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2009<!--]--></a>). Co-occurrence networks are gaining popularity in microbial ecology (Faust and Raes, <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B42-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B42a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></span>), and recently have been applied to observational studies of marine and soil systems (Steele et al., <a href="#B140" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2011<!--]--></a>; Barberan et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B9-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><span id="B9a" class="ArticleReference__scrollTarget" aria-hidden="true"></span><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></span>; Eiler et al., <span role="button" tabindex="0" id="B36-button" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></span>; Gilbert et al., <a href="#B55" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>). Network analysis applied to controlled experiments can provide insight into the associations between community members that are lost, gained, or maintained after a disturbance (Shade et al., <a href="#B131" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>). Networks can also be used to discover “core” community members shared across communities from similar habitats (Shade and Handelsman, <a href="#B132" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>), serving as a method to identify taxa shared across localities within a larger metacommunity.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--[--><p>Theoretical and empirical work on food webs indicate that the robustness of such networks is affected by several attributes, such as the strength of links among species (Montoya et al., <a href="#B104" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2006<!--]--></a>). In particular, architectural properties of trophic networks affect the relationship between network complexity and stability (May, <a href="#B100" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1974<!--]--></a>; Pimm, <a href="#B114" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1984<!--]--></a>; McCann et al., <a href="#B101" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->1998<!--]--></a>; Rozdilsky and Stone, <a href="#B123" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2001<!--]--></a>). For example, in mutualistic networks, compositional diversity and connectivity lead to higher resilience, whereas these properties destabilize trophic networks (Thébault and Fontaine, <a href="#B147" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>). Microbial communities are probably affected by both mutualistic and trophic interactions, and thus may provide a unique system for exploring the relationship between network attributes and community stability. Though we hypothesize that microbial interactions and the emergent network properties of a microbial community likely contribute to both resistance and resilience to pulse and press disturbances (Figure <a href="#F4" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->4<!--]--></a>), the exact mechanisms underlying this stability often are unknown, and may be challenging to unravel for many species-rich microbial communities that maintain both mutualistic and trophic interactions among their members.</p><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--><!--[--><!--]--><!--]--><!--]--></div><div id="h6"><!--[--><h2>Outlook: Communities as Systems of Genes and their Functions</h2><p>Microbial ecology is in a unique position in the larger field of ecology. Since the inception of community ecology, studies of the nature of communities at all taxonomic levels have been challenged by common difficulties. Producing a complete census, controlling variables, sampling completeness, and accounting for low abundance members are typical problems that have confronted all community ecologists, including microbial ecologists. However, the advent of meta-omics has provided microbiologists with the tools to address each of these challenges in new ways (Gilbert et al., <a href="#B54" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2010<!--]--></a>; Teeling et al., <a href="#B146" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>). Portraits of a community’s genes, gene expression, and metabolite production can be represented in a single sample, providing insight into system-level stability. Consequently, microbial ecologists are in a position to elucidate global principles in a manner that is not easily available in the broader field of ecology.</p><p>For example, time series of 16S rRNA, shotgun metagenomics, meta-transcriptomics, and meta-metabolomics data will allow researchers to quantify the number of functions shared across taxa from the same community, identify the taxa that are expressing genes for those functions at a given time point, and determine the functional output (in terms of number, abundance, and composition of molecules) from those transcripts. Analyzing this suite of information through time and in response to disturbances will provide quantitative insight as to how often and under what scenarios microbial community structure and function are linked, and whether those linkages are relevant for ecosystem processes. Applying this suite of tools to carefully designed disturbance experiments will additionally help to unravel mechanisms of community stability into different habitats. It will also provide key insights into defining ecologically relevant taxonomic and functional units for microorganisms. Thus, with information-rich datasets, precisely collected time series, and thoughtfully designed experiments (Knight et al., <a href="#B76" class="ArticleReference" data-event="dt_articles-click-open_reference"><!--[--><!--]--><!--[-->2012<!--]--></a>), microbial ecologists are poised to test fundamental hypotheses in ecology, and to move forward in predicting stability of microbial communities in the face of novel disturbances.</p><!--]--></div><div id="h7"><!--[--><h2>Supplementary Material</h2><p>The Supplementary Material for this article can be found online at <!--[--><a href="http://www.frontiersin.org/Fractal_Physiology/10.3389/fphys.2012.00417/abstract">http://www.frontiersin.org/Fractal_Physiology/10.3389/fphys.2012.00417/abstract</a><!--]--></p><!--]--></div><!--]--><!--[--><h2 id="h8"> Statements </h2><!--[--><div id="" class="Statement__Acknowledgments"><h3>Acknowledgments</h3><!--[--><p>We thank the ISME13 2010 roundtable selection committee for providing discussion space for the topic of microbial resilience. of quantitative definitions of resistance and resilience from ecology (Westman, 1978; Orwin and Wardle, 2004; Suding et al., 2004). A microbial community parameter of interest has a mean value of y0 and temporal variance, illustrated here by a 95% confidence interval around the mean (though other quantifications of variance, such as standard deviation or variance ratios may be used). A pulse disturbance ends (or a press disturbance begins) at time t0 and the parameter changes by |y0 − yL| after a time lag tL − t0. Resistance (RS) is an index of the magnitude of this change. (1)RS=1−2|y0−yL|y0+|y0−yL| Resilience (RL) is an index of the rate of return to y0 after the lag period, (2)RL=[2|y0−yL||y0−yL|+|y0−yn|−1]÷(tn−tL) where yn is the parameter value at measurement time tn. A parameter is “recovered” when it is statistically indistinguishable from the pre-disturbance mean. Alternatively, the parameter may not recover and instead may stabilize at a new mean value representing an alternative stable state. This possibility is more likely in response to a press disturbance. Over decades of ecological research many processes involved in shaping ecological communities have been described. Vellend ( 2010 ,  2016 ) states that virtually all processes fit under one or more of the following four so‐called higher level processes: (1) Selection; (2) Dispersal; (3) Drift and (4) Speciation. These processes can be either stochastic, like drift, or deterministic, as selection or both, for example, speciation and dispersal (Chase and Myers  2011 ; Stegen et al.  2012 ; Vellend et al.  2014 ).
In microbial communities, there is strong support for the idea that deterministic processes are very important for community assembly (Martiny et al.  2006 ; Lindström and Langenheder  2012 ; Nemergut et al.  2013 ; Langenheder and Lindström  2019 ). For example, selection is a deterministic process where fitness differences between individuals from different species lead to changes in community composition in response to environmental filtering via abiotic factors and species interactions (Vellend  2010 ,  2016 ) and is commonly observed (e.g., Langenheder and Lindström  2019 ). On the contrary, stochastic processes were originally thought to be less important in microbial community assembly, but have gained increasing attention (Zhou and Ning  2017 ). It now acknowledged that deterministic and stochastic processes simultaneously can affect microbial community assembly (Santillan et al.  2025 ). For example, studies have shown that initially similar communities diverge over time under similar environmental conditions, indicating that stochasticity, including processes such as drift related to random birth and death events, can also play an important role (Zhou et al.  2013 ; Gundersen et al.  2021 ).
Environmental disturbances can reduce microbial diversity and the ecosystem processes they mediate (Steudel et al.  2012 ). Salinity, in particular, strongly influences microbial diversity and community composition (Song et al.  2022 ). This can be important in estuarine environments, where freshwater and seawater mix and salinity gradients fluctuate greatly (Lozupone and Knight  2007 ). However, the specific consequences of such disturbances for bacterial communities remain less well understood (Graham et al.  2016 ). Current evidence suggests that disturbed bacterial communities are often predominantly shaped by deterministic processes, driven by increased selection pressure, which can reduce local diversity (Wang et al.  2022 ; Chen et al.  2023 ; Odhiambo et al.  2023 ; Dai et al.  2023 ). Several experimental studies support this pattern (Gundersen et al.  2021 ; Santillan et al.  2019 ), and in some cases, bacterial communities may not fully recover from disturbances (Santillan et al.  2020 ). However, intermediate levels of disturbance can increase stochasticity in community assembly, resulting in less predictable outcomes, and also affect community functioning (Santillan et al.  2019 ; Santillan and Wuertz  2022 ).
The filtering effect of past disturbances on community composition might ‘protect’ communities from the effects of subsequent disturbances through stress‐induced community tolerance (Blanck  2002 ; Vinebrooke et al.  2003 ) or acquired stress resistance (Rillig et al.  2015 ; Andrade‐Linares et al.  2016 ), ultimately shaping the adaptive capacity of ecosystems (Angeler et al.  2019 ). Such legacies of past disturbances might also be transient, creating a ‘short memory’ (Cabrol et al.  2016 ; Vass and Langenheder  2017 ). ‘Memory’ should here be understood as a phenomenon including several different processes, such as adaptations and selection of different individuals possessing certain traits as a result of a past disturbance (Johnstone et al.  2016 ). In general, little is known about how time since last disturbance, as well as other properties of past disturbances, affect the ability of microbial communities to cope with subsequent disturbances (Philippot et al.  2021 ). More specifically, it is unclear when legacy effects increase the adaptive capacity or when they, on the contrary, erode it, leading to a persistent reorganization of community structure and function.
We aimed to determine how previous pulse disturbances, and the recovery time since the last disturbance, shape bacterial community responses to a new, stronger disturbance. Community responses were quantified as changes in alpha‐ and beta‐diversity. We hypothesized that these changes arising as a result of a disturbance would be reduced in communities with a history of previous exposure to the same type of disturbance. Moreover, we hypothesized that this protective memory effect of disturbance history would be transient and weaken with a longer time elapsed since last disturbance. To test our hypotheses, we cultivated a freshwater bacterioplankton community in continuous culture, creating different exposure histories of repeated minor salinity pulses followed by long and short recovery periods, and a subsequent major salinity pulse disturbance (Figure  1a , see methods for more details).
(a) Experimental set‐up showing the 3 × 2 treatment groups, three different disturbance histories (control, long and short recovery time) with each pulse and no pulse conditions. Each treatment was replicated four times. (b) Expected variation between replicates over time for the different treatments (shown in different colours and line types). Blue shaded area shows the timing of the minor salinity pulses for the long disturbance history and red for the short disturbance history, whereas the grey shaded area shows the timing of the major salinity pulse.
(a) Experimental set‐up showing the 3 × 2 treatment groups, three different disturbance histories (control, long and short recovery time) with each pulse and no pulse conditions. Each treatment was replicated four times. (b) Expected variation between replicates over time for the different treatments (shown in different colours and line types). Blue shaded area shows the timing of the minor salinity pulses for the long disturbance history and red for the short disturbance history, whereas the grey shaded area shows the timing of the major salinity pulse.
In addition to selection based on ‘memory’ effects, our experiment allowed us to evaluate the possible influence of stochasticity. The latter should manifest, given dispersal was limited, as variation among replicates that cannot be systematically attributed to the disturbance history treatments. Based on previous research (Evans et al.  2017 ) we expect that stochasticity in our experiment would be visible as (1) increased beta‐diversity among communities (across replicates within a treatment) over time, and (2) increased importance of stochasticity compared to determinism in community assembly as shown through null modelling. Further, we hypothesized that stochasticity, and, thus, divergence between the replicates, would be temporarily halted or reduced for the duration of the series of minor disturbances in the long and short recovery treatments and for the duration of the major pulse disturbance in all disturbance history treatments (Figure  1b ). During the remainder of the study period, this divergence was expected to continue at a steady rate.
The experiment was performed with bacterioplankton communities grown in a continuous culture setup. There were 3 × 2 treatment groups, with four replicates each (24 vessels in total, Figure  1a ). Three different exposure histories (eight vessels per disturbance history treatment) were created during the first 27 days of the experiment by administering a series of three minor salinity disturbances (5 ppt NaCl each) with 3 days between the 1st and 2nd minor pulse and 5 days between the 2nd and 3rd minor pulse, and varying recovery times. The ‘long recovery treatment’ and ‘short recovery treatment’ were followed by two‐ and one‐week recovery periods, respectively, after the last minor pulse, while the ‘background treatment’ served as the control for this factor and was left undisturbed during this period (Figure  1a ). Half (4) of the replicates from each disturbance history treatment were then exposed to a single, stronger, salinity pulse (15 ppt NaCl). After this disturbance, the communities were allowed to grow in continuous culture for an additional 23 days under background laboratory conditions. Considering the origin of the bacterial community (see below), we did not expect any previous exposure to salinity, so that any salinity addition would likely be a disturbance. The strengths of the salinity pulses were chosen based on results from previous experiments conducted at our laboratory using freshwater bacteria (Berga et al.  2012 ), which indicated that salinity changes of c. 5 and > 10 PSU constitute intermediate and strong disturbances, respectively. The timing of the disturbances was chosen in relation to the generation time of the bacterial community in continuous culture, where we aimed to allow at least one generation to pass between each of the repeated minor disturbances, and to allow several generations to pass between the disturbance history and the major pulse. The goal, by doing this, was to focus on community level processes, rather than mainly physiological (within one generation) or evolutionary (over the course of many generations) processes.
Since the salt was gradually diluted out of the vessels due to the continuous culture setup, it is not straightforward to determine exactly when the disturbances ended. However, we estimate that the disturbances ended at the latest 4 days after the last minor salinity pulse and 6 days after the major pulse, as that is when the conductivity levels returned to below 1500 μS/cm, which is the high end of the conductivity range associated with freshwater (data not shown). Note that samples for analysis of the bacterial communities were always taken before disturbances were applied.
The bacterial community used to initiate the experimental communities was collected in a sterile bottle from a freshwater forest stream in the Uppland region of Sweden (59°55′05.0″ N, 17°20′49.2″ E). The site was upstream of Lake Fiby (conductivity: 9.60 mS m −1 ; pH: 7.30; alkalinity/acidity: 0.516 mekv L −1 ; total organic carbon: 27.9 mg L −1  C; total nitrogen: 1070 μg L −1  N; total phosphorus: 37.9 μg L −1  P; (Miljödata‐MVM 2020)). The microbial community was filtered through 0.7 μm filters (Whatman GF/F grade filters), to remove potential predatory organisms, and was then allowed to acclimatize at laboratory conditions. The acclimatization consisted of 4 days in batch culture, without added medium, followed by 3 weeks in continuous culture under the same conditions as during the main experiment. Each culture vessel contained 200 mL of the bacterial community growing in medium. We used an artificial lake water medium, made according to Bastviken et al. ( 2004 ). As a carbon source, we used 10 mg L −1  autoclaved dissolved organic carbon collected from the same stream used to source the starting communities using a reverse osmosis machine (Realsoft, Norcross, GA, USA). Medium was pumped through the vessels at a continuous rate of 70.4 μL min −1  throughout the experiment, which equals a dilution rate of 0.02 h −1  and a generation time of 32.8 h. The dilution rate is the medium flow rate divided by the culture volume and the generation time is ln(2) divided by the dilution rate (Ziv et al.  2013 ). In order to counteract any divergence between the communities that might have occurred during acclimation, we homogenized the communities from the 24 vessels and redistributed them before starting the experiment. The experiment took place at 20°C and in the dark. The communities were stirred using magnetic stirrers to prevent flocculation and formation of biofilms in the vessels (Ziv et al.  2013 ).
Every second day 20 mL samples were taken from all replicates for analysis. The samples were taken from the water column through a mounted syringe connected to a three‐way stop‐cock valve to avoid contamination while regulating access to the vessels. A solution of 350 g L −1  NaCl was prepared and autoclaved before adding 2.86 or 11.44 mL to each vessel to reach the intended disturbance intensities of 5 ppt and 15 ppt NaCl, respectively.
To control for possible effects of the physical disturbance associated with addition of the salt solution, all replicates not receiving a salinity pulse at any given disturbance point instead received autoclaved Milli‐Q water identical to the volume of the salt solution added to the disturbed communities. All salinity pulse disturbances and control treatments were administered using the mounted syringe described above. Each vessel had an air tube with a 0.2 μm air filter to prevent pressure buildup in the system.
For community composition analysis, 10 mL of culture from each community was filtered onto a 0.2 μm filter (PALL) to collect the bacterial cells. The filters were stored at −80°C while awaiting processing. DNA was extracted from the filters using DNeasy Powersoil DNA extraction kits (Qiagen, Maryland, USA) and stored at −20°C until further processing. The 16S rRNA genes (V3 and V4 regions) were amplified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) in two steps (see Methods  S1  for detailed information). Sequencing was performed by the SNP&SEQ Technology Platform (Illumina MiSeq, v.3 sequencing chemistry) in Uppsala. Demultiplexed sequence data from the 624 samples collected during the experiment were processed using the DADA2 pipeline (DADA2 R package version 1.8, using R version 3.4.3, (Callahan et al.  2016 )). The sequences were truncated after 290 nucleotides for forward and 240 for reverse reads. Amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were identified and chimeras were removed after merging read pairs, leading to 16% chimera removal. Taxonomy was assigned to the ASVs using the SILVA SSU 132 reference database.
Samples with fewer than 10,000 reads (23 samples out of 624) were excluded from further analysis. This resulted in 1304 ASV's and an average of 23,753 reads per sample. All analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.2). To account for the compositional nature of the ASV data, we followed the framework proposed by Gloor et al.  2017 . For ASV richness, sequencing depth was standardized across samples by randomly subsampling ASVs to 10,245 reads per sample using  rrarefy  from the vegan package (version 2.6‐8, Figure  S1 ). This rarefaction step was performed to minimize biases arising from unequal sequencing depth among samples and to enable comparable diversity estimates. To quantify temporal changes in ASV richness after the major pulse disturbance across the different treatments (control, short and long recovery history), we used log response ratios (LRR; Hedges et al.  1999 ). For each treatment (control, long and short recovery history), we computed:
where values close to zero indicate similarity to no major pulse conditions, and larger positive or negative values indicate stronger deviation from no major pulse conditions. We focused the LRR analysis on ASV richness because richness directly reflects ASV turnover following disturbance and provides an interpretable measure of community‐level change. To account for natural variability among replicates, LRRs were also calculated among no‐major‐pulse replicates.
To visualize overall treatment effects on community composition, we performed a principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) with Aitchison distances, the Euclidean distance over centred log‐ratio (CLR) transformed data, on the global ASV data. This approach is appropriate for compositional microbiome data because it accounts for the relative nature of sequence counts. To test the effects of disturbance history, major‐pulse treatment, time and their interactions on community structure, we performed factorial PERMANOVA on Aitchison distance matrices using adonis2 in the vegan package with 999 permutations. Analyses were conducted across the complete experiment and separately for the periods before (Days 1–27) and after (Days 28–50) the major pulse. Time was included as a continuous predictor, and model terms were evaluated sequentially (by = ‘terms’). Homogeneity of multivariate dispersion was assessed for disturbance history, major‐pulse treatment where applicable, and sampling time using PERMDISP (betadisper) on the corresponding Aitchison distance matrices. Distances to group centroids were calculated, and significance was evaluated using 999 permutations. To evaluate differences between replicates per treatment and time point, we used pairwise Aitchison distance on the original abundances using  robust aitchison  implemented in  vegdist  in the vegan package (Martino et al.  2019 ). This approach first replaces zeros with a small pseudocount, equal to half of the minimum nonzero relative abundance, and then applies CLR transformation. Euclidean distances are then computed in this CLR space. This approach quantifies proportional differences in community composition and is appropriate for compositional data (Aitchison  1982 ; Aitchison et al.  2000 ).
To assess the relative roles of stochastic versus deterministic processes in community assembly, we performed null model analysis using the normalized stochasticity ratio (NST; Ning et al.  2019 ). NST compares the observed community dissimilarity, abundance‐weighted Aitchison distances computed with the robust Aitchison method, to a distribution of dissimilarities generated under a specified null model. We used  tNST  in package NST (version 3.1.10) with a Proportional‐Fixed (PF) null model and 999 randomizations. NST values range from 0 to 1 and reflect the relative balance between deterministic and stochastic assembly processes, with lower values indicating a stronger relative contribution of deterministic processes and higher values indicating a stronger relative contribution of stochastic processes.
Linear mixed‐effects models (LMM) were used to evaluate how disturbance history (i.e., control, long recovery and short recovery treatments) and the major salinity pulse affected each of our response variables (Table  S1 ). We conducted two sets of LMMs, the first focused on samples conducted prior to the major salinity pulse (i.e., with only samples collected before Day 27 were included) and a second focused on samples collected after the major salinity pulse. ASV richness prior to the major pulse was modelled as a function of disturbance history, sampling day and their interaction as fixed effects, with replicate identity included as a random intercept. Prior to the major salinity pulse, each disturbance‐history treatment consisted of  n  = 8 replicates sampled repeatedly through time. Because the major pulse had not yet been applied, replicates that were later assigned to the major‐pulse and no‐major‐pulse treatments were analysed together within each disturbance‐history treatment.
For LMMs of samples collected after the major salinity pulse on Day 27, the analysis included  n  = 4 replicate per treatment, with ASV richness analysed using log‐response ratios (LRR), calculated as the difference between major‐pulse and no‐major‐pulse treatments within each disturbance‐history treatment. LRRs were modelled as a function of disturbance history, with sampling day included as a random intercept. To assess treatment effects on pairwise Aitchison distances and normalized stochasticity ratios (NST) before and after the major pulse, linear mixed‐effects models included disturbance history, centred sampling day, major pulse treatment (when applicable) and their interactions as fixed effects. Pairwise comparison identity or replicate identity was included as a random effect, depending on the response variable, to account for repeated sampling through time. Continuous predictors were centred where appropriate to aid interpretation. Degrees of freedom and  p ‐values were estimated using Satterthwaite's approximation implemented in the lmerTest package. Model residuals were visually inspected to confirm assumptions of homoscedasticity and normality. Because analyses were hypothesis‐driven and response variables represented distinct ecological properties,  p ‐values were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
ASV richness declined across all treatments during the early phase of the experiment, reaching a minimum prior to the major pulse on Day 27 (Figure  S2 ). Prior to the major salinity pulse (Day 27), disturbance history, time and their interaction significantly affected ASV richness (Table  1 ). ASV richness declined over time in all treatments during the early phase of the experiment (Figure  S2 ). After the major pulse on Day 27, richness remained relatively stable in the control and long recovery treatments, whereas stronger temporal fluctuations were observed in the short recovery treatment. Overall, post‐pulse richness remained below initial levels across treatments (Figure  S2 ). To assess the effect of the major pulse across disturbance histories, we used log response ratio (LRR) of ASV richness for each recovery history (control, long and short recovery; Figure  2 ) comparing communities receiving a major pulse with those that did not. Both the long and short recovery treatments showed significantly higher LRR values compared to the undisturbed control (Table  2 ). Thus, communities with a history of disturbance increased in richness after the major pulse with the short recovery treatment showing the strongest positive response (Figure  2 ). In contrast, communities lacking disturbance history (i.e., controls) decreased in richness if receiving the major pulse.
