PERMANOVA revealed that disturbance history, major pulse, time and all their interaction significantly affected community composition (Table  S2 ). PERMDISP showed that, across all time points, multivariate dispersion differed significantly among disturbance‐history treatments, between major‐pulse treatments and among sampling times (Table  S3 ). Additionally, PCoA ordination indicates that time was a major factor structuring community composition with an increase in beta‐diversity over time (Figure  3 , Figure  S4a–c ). Variation among replicate communities was also evident in their taxonomic composition at the final sampling day. Relative abundances at the phylum level showed distinct compositional differences among replicates within each disturbance‐history treatment (Figure  S3 ).

We calculated pairwise Aitchison distances within each treatment and time point to quantify the divergence between replicates. Before the major pulse, pairwise Aitchison distances increased over time and slopes increased significantly more in both the long and short recovery treatments compared to the undisturbed control (Figure  4 ; Table  2 ), although the magnitude of these differences was relatively small. After the major pulse, Aitchison distances became flatter across treatments. There was a significant effect of disturbance history and the major pulse on Aitchison distance, as well as the interaction between the major pulse and disturbance history (Table  2 ). More specifically, in treatments with a disturbance history (both long and short recovery) Aitchison distances were higher in treatments receiving the major pulse compared to those not receiving it, while no such effect was visible in treatments without a disturbance history (Figure  4 ).

Results from the null model analysis showed that NST values exceeded 0.5 across all treatments and at nearly all time points (Figure  5 ). Prior to the major pulse, NST increased significantly over time, and both disturbance history treatments exhibited higher NST values than the undisturbed control (Table  2 ). Following the major pulse, disturbance history remained associated with differences in NST (Table  2 ; Figure  5 ), and the pulse itself had a close to significant effect ( p  = 0.094). The interaction between disturbance history and the major pulse was significant only for the long recovery treatment, in which communities exposed to the major pulse displayed consistently higher NST values than those that did not receive the pulse (Figure  5 ; Table  2 ).

355: Microbial communities are at the heart of all ecosystems, and yet microbial community behavior in disturbed environments remains difficult to measure and predict. Understanding the drivers of microbial community stability, including resistance (insensitivity to disturbance) and resilience (the rate of recovery after disturbance) is important for predicting community response to disturbance. Here, we provide an overview of the concepts of stability that are relevant for microbial communities. First, we highlight insights from ecology that are useful for defining and measuring stability. To determine whether general disturbance responses exist for microbial communities, we next examine representative studies from the literature that investigated community responses to press (long-term) and pulse (short-term) disturbances in a variety of habitats. Then we discuss the biological features of individual microorganisms, of microbial populations, and of microbial communities that may govern overall community stability. We conclude with thoughts about the unique insights that systems perspectives – informed by meta-omics data – may provide about microbial community stability.
368: Here, we introduce a breadth of topics that provide insight into the responses of microbial communities to disturbance. We first highlight key concepts from ecology that are useful in thinking about microbial stability, pointing readers to an extensive literature on the subject of disturbance and community stability. We then summarize the current state of knowledge about resistance and resilience of microbial communities inhabiting a variety of ecosystems, emphasizing overarching trends gleaned from a review of 247 representative studies. We next provide a synthesis of the properties of individual microorganisms, populations, and communities that influence microbial community stability. Finally, we discuss insights into stability that may emerge from a systems-level perspective – describing microbial communities as networks of genes, transcripts, proteins, and metabolite signals.
